candidates.text:
“One of my biggest fears is coming out of Q4 and not feeling like we are smarter heading into next year strategy wise.” -our very wise client @RobPerry_ 

Tomorrow Sept 10, @ridgewallet, @hexclad, AppLovin, and I are hanging out for a live masterclass on Q4 planning.

@Seanfrank and @couuor are pulling back the curtain on Ridge's holiday gift campaigns. 

HexClad's @connorrolain and @londonspilker are sharing how they're driving net-new customers. 

And I’ll share a little of what we’ve learned over 5 years of BFCM testing at Haus. 

A little sneak peak:

DELAYED LIFT EXCEEDED IMMEDIATE LIFT IN 73% OF EXPERIMENTS 
Translation: day-to-day performance indicators only represent a fraction of the impact of your media during Q4, when consumers are largely waiting to see what kind of discount or offer they’ll get. The majority of impact from your paid video and social ads in particular will come weeks after they’re live. 

VIDEO CAMPAIGNS DROVE 286% MORE DELAYED LIFT THAN SEARCH
Video campaigns across YT and CTV drove the most disproportionately delayed impact among all channels we analyzed. Awareness campaigns on social drove a bit less than half of video, followed by paid social conversion campaigns and then paid search well below the rest. 

DELAYED LIFT INCREASES BY 79% DURING Q4
These effects seem to be more pronounced during Q4 than the rest of the year, based on a comparison to tests on the same channels for the brands we studied. Conversion campaigns on paid social and search saw the most pronounced increase relative to evergreen periods - in other words, even typically very direct response tactics become start to be more effective at building the funnel during Q4.

candidates.text:
.@rabois on the AI doom discourse:

"There's a question of whether these people should be building or working there, or forfeiting their equity if they really believe they're doing something that's bad or evil."

"In my opinion, the world is getting a little tired of some of this."

"We had the gloom and doom about jobs — 'All jobs are going away. There won't be any jobs left for humans.'"

"It could still happen, but all the evidence as of today is to the contrary. Every single piece of evidence. You can't find any evidence that AI is creating job loss. If anything, it's creating jobs."

"Then they're like, 'Oh my God, the world's going to end.' Ok, well, it's hard to falsify that. With AI and jobs, at least you can falsify it. But this one's a little harder to falsify."

"Articulate how the world ends. Because then, at least, we can start trying to falsify the predicates. And prove or try to disprove that there's some risk there."

"The burden is on people arguing for regulation or slowing things down to articulate what goes wrong, why, and how, so that people can probe, push back, and try to evaluate that risk."

"And I've yet to see a compelling answer to that, that's not just like, 'I know because I was working on it, and it's really dangerous.'"

candidates.text:
Vals AI CEO Rayan Krishnan on how they score a model's ability to build its own successor:

"One benchmark we released recently is our Recursive Self-Improvement Index. It's a topic which a lot of the big labs have been talking about and starting to report on in their model cards."

"There isn't a shared language to talk about the RSI potential of models. So we created this as an apples-to-apples way to actually benchmark across the models."

"In an ideal world, what you want to do is take a frontier model and have it train the next version of itself and see where the delta comes from. But obviously that's very expensive and slow."

"What we're doing is forming a set of proxies for every part of the process it takes to build the next version of the model."

"There's work around pre-training, post-training, harness-level engineering, and then seeing in which mechanisms and behaviors the models are able to do very good research work and build something new, and where they're struggling."

@RayanKrishnan @JenniferHli

candidates.text:
Vals AI CEO Rayan Krishnan on why defensible evals are critical for enterprises' survival:

"The labs side of it is very clear. If you're raising lots of money, investing heavily in building models, it's essential for you to show why your model is getting better and why the customer should pay a premium for them."

"But what I think is still underappreciated is, on the enterprise side, this is turning out to be existential as well."

"We're in this world where it is still very unclear what ROI looks like and how to value this intelligence that's being used... Token spend may start to eclipse salary spend."

"If this is such a meaningful line item in your costs, you have to justify the ROI much more cleanly... Over time, I think a firm really is just its evals."

"The ability for a company to make its evals legible in order to solve this ROI calculus is going to be the reason why that company wins out over its competitors in the long term."

@RayanKrishnan @eriktorenberg
